You are reading the learner view -- the course as a learner sees it. The design document, mentor guide and quiz solutions are not included.

A course applying a systematic troubleshooting framework (Clarify the Problem → Understand the Context → Reproduce the Problem → Test Systematically → Know When to Escalate) to translation software issues, alongside guidance for supporting translators effectively while doing so.

Originally backfilled from Cypher for Business (see BACKFILL.md), this course has since entered the 8-stage production pipeline — see 00-design.md.

docs.title: Software Support and Troubleshooting for Translation Teams
docs.text:
Estimated time: 55 minutes

Level: 1 - Has Knowledge

Purpose: Apply a systematic approach to diagnosing and resolving translation software issues while supporting translators effectively.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Time: 10 minutes

Imagine you receive this message from a translator:

"Help! Nothing is working. I was translating yesterday and everything was fine, but today when I opened the program, my work isn't showing up. I have a deadline tomorrow and I'm panicking. What do I do?"

docs.title: Reflection Question
docs.text:
Think about a time when someone asked you for technical help (or when you needed help yourself). What made the situation more stressful or more manageable? What questions would you want to ask to understand what's actually happening?

✏️ Reflection: Take a moment to consider: What's your natural response when someone brings you a problem like this? Do you jump straight to solutions, ask lots of questions first, or feel overwhelmed by not knowing the answer immediately? Add your response to your learning journal.

docs.title: Content
docs.text: Time: 30 minutes

docs.title: Section 1: The Reality of Translation Software Support
docs.text:
When supporting translation teams, you'll encounter issues ranging from simple misunderstandings ("I can't find the button") to complex technical problems ("the synchronization is corrupted"). The challenge is that you often won't know everything about every tool, and that's okay.

Key Point: Effective support isn't about knowing all the answers immediately—it's about knowing how to systematically figure out what's wrong and where to find help when needed.

Your role combines three essential elements: - Technical troubleshooting skills - Understanding of translator workflows and context - Clear, empathetic communication

docs.title: Section 2: The Systematic Troubleshooting Framework
docs.text:
When a translator reports a problem, use this framework to diagnose and resolve issues effectively:

1. Clarify the Problem

Before you can solve anything, you need to understand exactly what's happening. Panicked messages like "nothing works" or "it's broken" are starting points, not complete problem descriptions.

Ask clarifying questions: - What were you trying to do? (Understanding their goal) - What happened instead? (The actual behavior) - When did you first notice this? (Timeline helps identify causes) - Has anything changed recently? (Updates, new files, different location) - Can you show me exactly what you're seeing? (Screenshots, error messages, specific behaviors)

NOTE — Example: A translator says "Send/Receive isn't working." This could mean: - The button is grayed out (permissions issue) - It starts but never finishes (network/server problem) - It shows an error message (specific error to diagnose) - It completes but their changes aren't appearing (synchronization logic issue) - It completes but another user's changes aren't appearing (synchronization logic, or the other user hasn't run a send/receive) - They can't find where to click (user interface familiarity)

Each of these requires a different solution, so clarification is essential.

2. Understand the Context

Translation work has patterns and contexts that affect troubleshooting: - Project structure: Are they working with a team project or individual files? Is this a brand new project or one that's been running for years? - Collaboration setup: Are multiple people working on the same data? How are they sharing files? - Work environment: Are they in the field with limited connectivity, or in an office with stable internet? Are they using their own device or a shared computer? - Recent changes: Did something just get updated? New operating system? New software version? Someone new joined the project?

Understanding context helps you ask the right questions and identify likely causes faster.

3. Reproduce the Problem

Whenever possible, try to see the problem yourself or have the translator show you exactly what's happening. This helps you: - Verify what's actually occurring versus what they think is happening - Notice details they might not mention - Test potential solutions in real-time

Sometimes "it's not working" turns out to be "I'm clicking the wrong button" or "I'm looking in the wrong place." Screen sharing or working alongside them reveals this immediately.

4. Test Systematically

Rather than randomly trying things, work methodically: - Start with the simplest, most common causes - Change one thing at a time so you know what worked - Document what you've tried and the results - If something fixes the problem, make sure you understand why it fixed it

NOTE — Example: If a file won't open: 1. Can they open other files? (Is it this specific file or all files?) 2. Can someone else open this file? (Is it the file or their setup?) 3. Does it open on a different computer? (Is it their device or the file?) 4. Is there a backup they can try? (Can we work around the corrupted file?)

5. Know When to Escalate

You won't solve every problem immediately. Learn to recognize when you need to: - Consult someone more experienced - Contact software vendor support - Restore from backup and move forward - Find a workaround rather than a complete fix

Knowing your limits and being willing to ask for help is a strength, not a weakness.

docs.title: Section 3: Supporting Translators Effectively
docs.text:
Technical skills matter, but so does how you interact with people who are often stressed, on deadlines, and worried about losing work.

Acknowledge their stress: "I can hear this is really frustrating. Let's figure out what's happening together."

Explain what you're doing: "I'm going to ask you some questions to help me understand exactly what's going on. Then we'll work through this systematically."

Be honest about what you know and don't know: "I haven't seen this exact error before, but let me check a few things with you" is much better than pretending you know when you don't, or giving false reassurance.

Manage expectations: If you need time to research, say so: "I want to investigate this properly rather than guess. Can I get back to you in two hours with a solution or at least a clearer picture of what's happening?"

Document and share learning: When you solve a problem, document it. This helps you remember for next time and creates resources for the whole team. A simple document with "Problem / Symptoms / Solution" entries becomes invaluable.

docs.title: Section 4: Common Translation Software Issues
docs.text:
While every situation is unique, certain patterns appear frequently:

Synchronization issues: - Often caused by network interruptions, conflicting changes, corrupted project data, or a user sending/receiving to the wrong location (e.g., a USB drive instead of the internet server), so their changes never reach teammates - Usually requires checking the connection, reviewing conflict reports, verifying the send/receive location, or restoring from backup

Missing work or data: - Could be user didn't save, file permissions changed, working in wrong location, or actual data loss - Start by checking autosave locations, recent files, and backup systems

Installation and compatibility: - Operating system updates can break software, antivirus can block features, insufficient permissions - Check system requirements, update software, verify administrator rights

Performance problems: - Large projects, insufficient memory, background processes competing for resources - Investigate project size, available RAM, other running programs

User interface confusion: - Person can't find a feature that exists, interface changed after update - Often solved by screen sharing to see exactly what they're seeing

docs.title: Section 5: Building Your Support Toolkit
docs.text:
Effective support requires preparation:

Knowledge resources: - Software documentation and help files - User forums and community groups - Vendor support contacts - Internal team knowledge base

Diagnostic tools: - Screen sharing software for remote support - Log file analyzers when available - Backup and recovery systems - Test environments to replicate issues

Communication tools: - Clear question templates for gathering information - Screenshot annotation tools - Step-by-step instruction formats - Progress update templates for longer issues

Personal habits: - Keep notes on issues you've solved - Build relationships with experienced troubleshooters - Stay current on software updates and known issues - Practice explaining technical concepts in non-technical language

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text: Time: 10 minutes

docs.title: Scenario 1: The Panicked Translator
docs.text:
You receive this message: "Everything is gone! I opened my project this morning and all my work from the past week has disappeared! What happened?!"

✏️ Your task: Write out the first three questions you would ask to understand what's actually happening. Then identify what information you'd need before proposing any solutions.

TIP This is one of three practice scenarios for this course. When you've worked through it, continue with the scenario bank — it adds The Unclear Error and The Recurring Problem — and submit your written responses to your mentor for feedback.

docs.title: Change
docs.text: Time: 5 minutes

docs.title: Personal Action Plan
docs.text:
TIP Choose one area to focus on in your next support situation:

Option A - Framework Practice: Pick one step of the troubleshooting framework (Clarify, Understand Context, Reproduce, Test Systematically, or Escalate) and commit to doing it more thoroughly in your next support situation.

Option B - Resource Building: Create one specific tool or resource to help you provide better support (e.g., a question template, a documentation system, a knowledge base entry, a list of escalation contacts).

Option C - Communication Practice: Identify one communication habit you want to develop (acknowledging stress, managing expectations, explaining technical concepts clearly) and plan how you'll practice it.

✏️ Write down: - What you'll do differently in your next support situation - How you'll know if your approach is working - What support or resources you need to make this change

docs.title: Looking Ahead
docs.text:
As you support translation teams: - Remember that systematic troubleshooting is more valuable than memorizing every possible solution - Your communication and empathy matter as much as your technical skills - Building relationships with translators and other support people creates a stronger support network - Documenting what you learn makes you and your whole team more effective over time

The goal isn't to become an expert in every translation tool—it's to become skilled at figuring out problems systematically and supporting people effectively while you do it.

docs.title: Scenario bank
docs.text:
Estimated time: 15 minutes

Purpose: Applied practice scenarios you work through after the lesson content, before the quiz. Each one asks you to explain how you would approach a real support situation using the 5-step framework from the lesson (Clarify the Problem → Understand the Context → Reproduce the Problem → Test Systematically → Know When to Escalate). At the Has Knowledge level, the goal is to show clear, systematic thinking on paper — not to fix a live machine — so your written reasoning is the deliverable.

Format: the scenarios progress from foundational → intermediate → complex. Scenario F1 is also worked as the in-lesson Challenge; F1 and I1 are confirmed real field cases.

docs.title: For learners
docs.text:
• Read each scenario carefully.
  • Apply the 5-step troubleshooting framework from the lesson.
  • Write out your reasoning — the questions you would ask, the order you would work in, and why. Explaining your approach is the task; you are not expected to have a single "right" fix.
  • Submit your written responses to your mentor for feedback.

docs.title: For mentors
docs.text:
• Use the accompanying mentor guide for assessment criteria.
  • Look for systematic thinking, not just a "correct" answer.
  • Provide constructive feedback.

INFO — a note on realism. Scenarios F1 and I1 are confirmed situations the course's SME has seen in the field. Scenario C1 is illustrative and plausible but is not a confirmed field case — treat it as a realistic thinking exercise rather than a documented incident.

docs.title: Scenario F1: The Panicked Translator
docs.text:
Situation: You receive this message: "Everything is gone! I opened my project this morning and all my work from the past week has disappeared! What happened?!"

Context: The translator is on a deadline, working from a field location, and clearly distressed. You do not yet know anything about how their project is set up or what changed between yesterday and today.

Objectives exercised: 1.

Your task:

  1. Write out the first three clarifying questions you would ask to understand what is actually happening.
  2. Explain what information you would need before proposing any solution.
  3. Note how you would acknowledge the translator's stress while you gather that information.

docs.title: Scenario I1: The Unclear Error
docs.text:
Situation: A translator sends you a screenshot of an error message in a language you don't speak well, and says "I keep getting this error and I don't know what to do."

Context: You cannot easily read the error text, and you are supporting the translator remotely rather than sitting beside them.

Objectives exercised: 3.

Your task:

  1. Describe your troubleshooting approach — what would you do first, second, and third?
  2. Explain how you would gather reliable information when you can't easily read the error yourself (for example, by having the translator show you the problem happening rather than relying only on their description).
  3. Explain why directly observing or reproducing the problem is more dependable here than working from the translator's account alone.

docs.title: Scenario C1: The Recurring Problem
docs.text:
Situation: A translator contacts you saying "This keeps happening. Every few days my work gets stuck and I have to restart the program. Can you fix it permanently?"

Context: The problem is intermittent — it appears every few days rather than every time — which makes it harder to catch in the act. You will need to reason about what is "normal" for this team's workflow and how you would isolate an on-again, off-again fault.

Objectives exercised: 2, 4, 5.

Your task:

  1. Explain how you would approach diagnosing an intermittent problem, and what project- and workflow-context factors you would want to understand first (how the team works, how they collaborate, what recently changed) to judge what is normal versus abnormal.
  2. Describe the information you would gather to identify a pattern, and how you would test systematically — changing one thing at a time — rather than trying fixes at random.
  3. Explain what you would tell the translator about your process, including how you would recognise that the problem exceeds what you can resolve alone and what the appropriate next step would be (escalate, contact vendor support, restore from backup, or agree a workaround).

docs.title: Assessment quiz (12 questions)
docs.text: This quiz covers the systematic troubleshooting framework and common issue categories taught in 01-software-support-and-troubleshooting.md. It tests whether you can recognize and explain good support practice (this is a 1 - Has Knowledge course), not whether you can perform live troubleshooting. You need 80% (10/12) to pass.

docs.title: Section 1: Clarifying the Problem (Questions 1-3)
docs.text:
Question 1: A translator messages you: "Help! Nothing is working!" According to the framework, what is your first job before proposing any solution? - A) Ask clarifying questions to turn the vague report into a specific, diagnosable issue - B) Reinstall the software to rule out corruption - C) Escalate to a vendor immediately because "nothing" is a serious symptom - D) Restore the project from the most recent backup

Question 2: Which set of questions best reflects the clarifying questions the lesson recommends asking? - A) "Have you paid for support? Which version did you buy? Who is your administrator?" - B) "Whose fault is this? Did you follow the instructions? Did you read the manual?" - C) "What were you trying to do? What happened instead? When did you first notice it? Has anything changed recently? Can you show me what you're seeing?" - D) "Can you reinstall it? Can you restart the computer? Can you try a different file?"

Question 3: True or False: A message like "Send/Receive isn't working" is a complete problem description that you can act on directly. - A) True - B) False

docs.title: Section 2: Understanding the Context (Questions 4-5)
docs.text:
Question 4: Why does the framework treat understanding a team's context (project structure, collaboration setup, work environment, recent changes) as its own step? - A) Because vendors require this information before they will respond - B) Because context replaces the need to reproduce the problem - C) Because it helps you judge what is normal versus abnormal for that team and identify likely causes faster - D) Because it is only relevant for brand-new projects

Question 5: A translator reports that a teammate's changes aren't appearing in the shared project. Which context factor is most directly relevant to diagnosing this? - A) How much RAM the translator's computer has - B) The collaboration setup — how many people share the data and how they are sending/receiving it - C) The translator's typing speed - D) Which font the project uses

docs.title: Section 3: Reproducing the Problem (Questions 6-7)
docs.text:
Question 6: Why does the lesson recommend reproducing or directly observing the problem (for example, by screen-sharing) rather than relying only on the translator's verbal description? - A) It lets you verify what is actually happening, notice details they might not mention, and test solutions in real time - B) It creates a record for the vendor's support ticket - C) It is required before you are allowed to escalate - D) It guarantees the problem is the translator's fault, not the software's

Question 7: A translator insists "the program is broken." When you watch their screen, you see they are clicking in the wrong place. What does this illustrate about reproducing a problem? - A) That verbal descriptions are always deliberately misleading - B) That you should have escalated sooner - C) That the software should be reinstalled - D) That "it's not working" can turn out to be a UI/familiarity issue that direct observation reveals immediately

docs.title: Section 4: Testing Systematically and Escalating (Questions 8-10)
docs.text:
Question 8: What is the defining principle of systematic testing in the framework? - A) Try as many fixes as fast as possible until something works - B) Change one thing at a time, starting with the simplest common causes, and document the results - C) Always begin with the most complex possible cause - D) Change several settings at once to save time

Question 9: A file won't open. Which sequence best reflects the systematic, one-variable-at-a-time approach the lesson describes? - A) Reinstall the software, then reinstall the operating system, then buy a new computer - B) Delete the file and ask the translator to start over - C) Can they open other files? Can someone else open this file? Does it open on a different computer? Is there a backup to try? - D) Wait a few days to see if the problem resolves itself

Question 10: Which of the following is a legitimate next step when a problem exceeds what you can resolve alone? - A) Consult someone more experienced - B) Contact software vendor support - C) Restore from backup or find a workaround rather than a complete fix - D) All of the above

docs.title: Section 5: Recognizing Common Issue Categories (Questions 11-12)
docs.text:
Question 11: A translator says: "My work saved fine yesterday, but today my project opens and a whole week of my translation is missing." Which common issue category does this description most closely match? - A) Missing work or data - B) Performance problems - C) Installation and compatibility - D) User interface confusion

Question 12: A translator reports that the program has become very slow since they started working on a large project, and that it lags when other applications are open. Which category — and which first checks — does the lesson associate with this? - A) Synchronization issues — check the connection and conflict reports - B) User interface confusion — screen-share to find the missing feature - C) Installation and compatibility — verify administrator rights and system requirements - D) Performance problems — investigate project size, available RAM, and other running programs

docs.title: How to review this
docs.text:
Work through the lessons in order, then the scenario bank, then the quiz, as a learner would. Note anything confusing or out of order.

Leave feedback as a comment on the course's pull request (line by line on the Files changed tab) or on its tracker issue. You do not need to edit anything yourself.
